summary: Describes a one-time password system for login and other uses that is secure against passive attacks based on replaying captured reusable passwords. It is an Internet standard and replaces RFC 1938.

plainLanguage.summary: Each password works only once. If a spy sees it go by, it is already used up and no good to them.

questions: what is a one-time password system
how does otp s/key authentication work
how does otp prevent replay attacks
subtitle: A login scheme where every password works exactly once, so a captured password is useless to an eavesdropper.

tldr.problem: Reusable passwords sent over a network can be captured by an eavesdropper and replayed later to get in.
tldr.mechanism: The user's secret pass-phrase and a server-supplied seed are run through a secure hash function a set number of times. The count drops by one after each login, and the server checks each password by hashing it once and comparing with the last one it accepted.
tldr.outcome: A captured password cannot be used again or used to guess the next one, though the system does nothing against active attacks such as session hijacking. It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 1938.

facts.label: Pass-phrase length
facts.value: At least 10 characters; 10 to 63 must be supported

today: RFC 2289 is an Internet Standard and obsoletes RFC 1938. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The Replay Problem and OTP
sections.content:
RFC 2289 describes the one-time password system (OTP), which evolved from Bellcore's S/KEY. It gives authentication for login and other uses that is secure against passive attacks based on replaying captured reusable passwords. An eavesdropper who records a login ID and password can use them later; that is called a replay attack.

Two parties take part. The generator produces the right one-time password from the user's secret pass-phrase and from a challenge. The server sends the challenge, verifies the password it gets back, stores the last valid one-time password and its sequence number, and must make it possible to change the pass-phrase securely. The secret pass-phrase never has to cross the network, and no secret needs to be stored on any system, including the server. The technique was first suggested by Leslie Lamport.
sections.plainLanguage: A secret phrase stays in your head. Each time you log in you show a different code made from it, and the computer never needs to keep your secret.

sections.title: The Secure Hash Function
sections.content:
The security of OTP rests on a secure hash function: easy to compute forwards, computationally infeasible to invert. Interfaces are defined for MD4, MD5 and SHA. All conforming servers and generators MUST support MD5, SHOULD support SHA and MAY support MD4. Both ends must use the same algorithm.

These hashes accept arbitrarily long input and give a fixed-size output. OTP folds that output down to 64 bits, which is also the length of a one-time password. The RFC calls this long enough to be secure and short enough to be entered by hand when necessary. Appendix A gives the folding code for each hash and requires the hash output to be stored in little endian format before the folding.
sections.plainLanguage: A hash is like a meat grinder: you can turn a steak into mince, but nobody can turn the mince back into the steak.

sections.title: Generating the Password Sequence
sections.content:
In the initial step, the pass-phrase is concatenated with a seed that the server sends in clear text. The result goes through the hash function and is folded to 64 bits, giving a value called S. The seed lets one pass-phrase be used on several machines with different seeds, and lets a user recycle a pass-phrase by changing the seed. Character-string pass-phrases MUST have at least 10 characters, and generators MUST support 10 to 63 characters.

In the computation step, the first password to be used is S hashed N times, where N is the count the user chose. The next password is S hashed N-1 times, and so on. An eavesdropper who sees one password cannot produce the next one without inverting the hash.

The seed MUST be alphanumeric, 1 to 16 characters long, free of blanks, and is converted to lower case before use. The seed and the sequence number together form the challenge.
sections.plainLanguage: You hash a secret over and over, and each login uses one step fewer. Going from step 50 to step 49 is easy for you but impossible for someone who only saw step 50.

sections.title: Challenge and Password Formats
sections.content:
A challenge has a fixed syntax so that automated generators can find it: otp-<algorithm identifier> <sequence integer> <seed>, for example otp-md5 487 dog2. The defined identifiers are md4, md5 and sha1.

The 64-bit password is hard to type, so it MAY be shown as six short words, each taken from a dictionary of 2048 words (11 bits per word). The two spare bits hold a checksum made by summing the 64 bits in pairs. Generators write the words in upper case separated by single spaces, for example OUST COAT FOAL MUG BEAK TOTE, and servers accept any case and spacing. All servers MUST also accept hexadecimal, and SHOULD accept an alternate-dictionary six-word form described in Appendix B. If an input is valid as six words it is accepted that way; otherwise it is tried as hexadecimal.
sections.plainLanguage: A long number is easy to mistype, so the code can be written as six short, common words, like a phrase you read out loud.

sections.title: How the Server Verifies a Password
sections.content:
The application on the server issues a challenge. The server keeps, for each user, the one-time password from the last successful authentication, or the first password of a newly initialised sequence. When a password arrives, the server decodes it to 64 bits and runs it through the hash function once. If the result matches the stored previous password, authentication succeeds and the new password is stored for next time.

Because the count falls by one each time, the user eventually has to reinitialise. Implementations MUST offer a way to do this that does not reveal the pass-phrase, and MUST check that the seed or the pass-phrase has changed. Installations SHOULD discourage sending the pass-phrase over a network in clear text. A suggested method has the user pick a new seed and hash count and supply the matching generated password.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer only remembers your last code. To check the new one, it does one hash step and sees whether it lands on the last code.

sections.title: Race Attacks and Limits of Protection
sections.content:
All conforming servers MUST protect against a race attack. An attacker can listen to most of a one-time password, guess the rest, and race the real user to finish. Multiple guesses against the last word of the six-word format are likely to succeed. One defence is to stop a user from starting several authentication sessions at once, with a timeout so the block cannot become a denial of service.

OTP only protects against passive eavesdropping and replay. It does not protect the privacy of transmitted data, nor against active attacks such as session hijacking; the RFC recommends IPsec against TCP session hijacking. It also depends on the hash functions staying non-invertible. The RFC says MD4 is generally believed to be weaker than MD5, and a server supporting several algorithms is only as secure as the weakest.
sections.plainLanguage: OTP stops a spy from reusing a code they overheard. It cannot stop someone who grabs your whole connection while you are logged in.
